Abstract

Reliable uncertainty quantification is critical for trustworthy AI. Conformal Prediction (CP) provides prediction sets with distribution-free coverage guarantees, but its two main variants face complementary limitations. Split CP (SCP) suffers from data inefficiency due to dataset partitioning, while full CP (FCP) improves data efficiency at the cost of prohibitive retraining complexity. Recent approaches based on meta-learning or in-context learning (ICL) partially mitigate these drawbacks. However, they rely on training procedures not specifically tailored to CP, which may yield large prediction sets. We introduce an efficient FCP framework, termed enhanced ICL-based FCP (E-ICL+FCP), which employs a permutation-invariant Transformer-based ICL model trained with a CP-aware loss. By simulating the multiple retrained models required by FCP without actual retraining, E-ICL+FCP preserves coverage while markedly reducing both inefficiency and computational overhead. Experiments on synthetic and real tasks demonstrate that E-ICL+FCP attains superior efficiency-coverage trade-offs compared to existing SCP and FCP baselines.

Index Terms: 
Conformal prediction, in-context learning, set prediction, few-shot learning

I Introduction

Reliable quantification of AI decision uncertainty is crucial in modern safety-critical applications [1, 2]. Bayesian learning and ensembling can quantify epistemic uncertainty [3, 4, 5], but their reliability degrades under model or prior misspecification [6, 7]. Moreover, exact Bayesian inference is computationally infeasible, while approximations such as Monte Carlo sampling [8] and variational inference [9] provide no formal reliability guarantees.

Conformal Prediction (CP) [10] is a post-hoc calibration framework that turns any arbitrary predictor – of a label yy given covariates 𝐱\mathbf{x} – into a reliable set predictor. The set predictor is guaranteed to contain the true label yy with probability at least 1−α1-\alpha, where α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1] is a user-specified significance level [11]. To elaborate, assume the availability of a dataset 𝒟={(𝐱i,yi)}i=1n\mathcal{D}=\{(\mathbf{x}_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} with the ii-th input 𝐱i∈𝒳\mathbf{x}_{i}\in\mathcal{X} and the corresponding discrete label yi∈𝒴={1,…,K}y_{i}\in\mathcal{Y}=\{1,\dots,K\}. Given a new test input 𝐱n+1\mathbf{x}_{n+1}, the CP predictive set 𝒞⁡(𝐱n+1)\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}) is constructed using data 𝒟\mathcal{D} so as to satisfy the following reliability condition

Pr​(yn+1∈𝒞⁡(𝐱n+1))⩾1−α,\text{Pr}(y_{n+1}\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}))\geqslant 1-\alpha, (1)

where the probability is evaluated with respect to the joint distribution of the data. The key performance metrics for CP are coverage and inefficiency: coverage corresponds to the left-hand side of (1), while inefficiency denotes the average size of the predictive set, i.e., 𝔼⁡[|𝒞⁡(𝐱n+1)|]\mathbb{E}[|\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{x}_{n+1})|].

Split CP (SCP) and full CP (FCP) are the two most common CP versions. SCP splits the dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} into a training set 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\text{tr}} and a calibration set 𝒟cal\mathcal{D}_{\text{cal}} [10]. However, data splitting may lead to an inefficient use of the available data 𝒟\mathcal{D}, resulting in high inefficiency when the available data is limited. In contrast, classical FCP uses the entire dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} for both training and calibration [12], thus achieving lower inefficiency, i.e., smaller predictive sets. On the flip side, the complexity of FCP is significantly higher, requiring retraining of a predictive model for each candidate label y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}.

To reduce SCP’s inefficiency, reference [13] proposed incorporating a regularizer based on the average set size into the training loss. Furthermore, the works [14, 15, 16] introduced meta-learning based CP schemes that improve efficiency of CP, while ensuring either an across-task validity guarantee [14, 15] or a per-task validity guarantee [16]. Proposals to decrease the computational cost of FCP include importance sampling in Bayesian learning [17] and in-context learning (ICL) [18].

ICL is a recent meta-learning paradigm [19] that builds upon pre-trained sequence models, like Transformers [20], enabling per-task adaptation without any parameter update. In this context, recent works [18, 21] were the first to employ ICL models to implement FCP [18], as well as the related cross-validation CP [21]. However, these works rely on conventional ICL training that is not optimized for CP, which can lead to large prediction sets.

In this work, we propose to meta-train a permutation-invariant ICL model explicitly tailored for FCP, aiming to yield more efficient predictive sets while provably meeting the coverage condition (1). Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed scheme, referred to as enhanced ICL-based FCP (E-ICL+FCP), achieves the desired coverage (1) with lower inefficiency, i.e., smaller predictive sets, and higher computational efficiency as compared to existing SCP and FCP baselines.

II Background

This section presents background on SCP, FCP, and ICL.

II-A Split Conformal Prediction

SCP splits the available data 𝒟={(𝐱i,yi)}i=1n\mathcal{D}=\{(\mathbf{x}_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} into a training set 𝒟tr={(𝐱i,yi)}i=1l\mathcal{D}_{\text{tr}}=\{(\mathbf{x}_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{l} and a calibration set 𝒟cal={𝐱i,yi}i=1m\mathcal{D}_{\text{cal}}=\{\mathbf{x}_{i},y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m}, where m+l=nm+l=n and 𝒟tr∩𝒟cal=∅\mathcal{D}_{\text{tr}}\cap\mathcal{D}_{\text{cal}}=\emptyset. The training dataset 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\text{tr}} is used to train a predictor p^​(y|𝐱)\hat{p}(y|\mathbf{x}) of the label yy given the covariates 𝐱\mathbf{x}. The predictor p^​(y|𝐱)\hat{p}(y|\mathbf{x}) is used to define a non-conformity score (NCS) function s⁡(𝐱,y)s(\mathbf{x},y) that quantifies how “unusual” a sample (𝐱,y)(\mathbf{x},y) is compared to the training data. A common NCS is the log-loss s⁡(𝐱,y)=−log⁡(p^​(y|𝐱))s(\mathbf{x},y)=-\log(\hat{p}(y|\mathbf{x})). More generally, the NCS can be a function of yy and the entire distribution p^(⋅|𝐱)\hat{p}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}) [11], but, to simplify the presentation, hereafter we will adopt the log-loss.

SCP computes the NCS values on the calibration set, obtaining the set 𝒮={s⁡(𝐱,y):(𝐱,y)∈𝒟cal}∪{∞}\mathcal{S}=\{\,s(\mathbf{x},y):(\mathbf{x},y)\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{cal}}\,\}\cup\{\infty\}, with an added fictitious data point having an infinite NCS. The prediction set is then obtained as

𝒞⁡(𝐱n+1)={y∈𝒴:s⁡(𝐱n+1,y)⩽Q1−α​(𝒮)},\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{x}_{n+1})=\{\,y\in\mathcal{Y}:s(\mathbf{x}_{n+1},y)\leqslant Q_{1-\alpha}(\mathcal{S})\}, (2)

where Q1−α​(⋅)Q_{1-\alpha}(\cdot) returns the (1−α)(1-\alpha)-quantile of the set 𝒮\mathcal{S}. This construction satisfies the coverage condition (1) [10].

II-B Full Conformal Prediction

In FCP, for each possible label y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}, we form an augmented dataset 𝒟y=𝒟∪{(𝐱n+1,y)}\mathcal{D}^{y}=\mathcal{D}\cup\{(\mathbf{x}_{n+1},y)\}. Then, a model p^y(⋅|𝐱)\hat{p}^{y}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}) is trained on each augmented dataset 𝒟y\mathcal{D}^{y}. The training algorithm is assumed to be permutation-invariant with respect to the data in 𝒟y\mathcal{D}^{y}, meaning that it yields the same model regardless of the order of the samples in 𝒟y\mathcal{D}^{y}. This condition is satisfied by standard stochastic gradient-based training algorithms that treat all training samples in the same way [22].

Using the |𝒴||\mathcal{Y}| trained models {p^y(⋅|𝐱)}y∈𝒴\{\hat{p}^{y}(\cdot|\mathbf{x})\}_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}, FCP computes the NCS values as siy=−log⁡(p^y​(yi|𝐱i))s_{i}^{y}=-\log(\hat{p}^{y}(y_{i}|\mathbf{x}_{i})) for i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n and sn+1y=−log⁡(p^y​(y|𝐱n+1))s_{n+1}^{y}=-\log(\hat{p}^{y}(y|\mathbf{x}_{n+1})) for each y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}. The predictive set for 𝐱n+1\mathbf{x}_{n+1} is then obtained by including all labels yy whose NCS sn+1ys_{n+1}^{y} is no greater than the (1−α)(1-\alpha)-quantile of the set {siy}i=1n+1\{s_{i}^{y}\}_{i=1}^{n+1}:

𝒞⁡(𝐱n+1)={y∈𝒴:sn+1y⩽Q1−α​({siy}i=1n+1)}.\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{x}_{n+1})=\left\{y\in\mathcal{Y}:s_{n+1}^{y}\leqslant Q_{1-\alpha}\left(\{s_{i}^{y}\}_{i=1}^{n+1}\right)\right\}. (3)

II-C In-Context Learning

Unlike conventional meta-learning methods [19], ICL exploits latent patterns in the context samples to adapt to new tasks without the need for explicit fine-tuning of model parameters for each task [23]. Given nn context examples 𝒟con={(𝐱i,yi)}i=1n\mathcal{D}_{\text{con}}=\{(\mathbf{x}_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} and a query input 𝐱n+1\mathbf{x}_{n+1}, an ICL model, G𝜽G_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}, parameterized by vector 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta} produces a predictive probability vector for 𝐱n+1\mathbf{x}_{n+1} as the output

p^(⋅|𝐱n+1)=G𝜽(𝒟con,𝐱n+1).{\hat{p}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}_{n+1})=G_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\left(\mathcal{D}_{\text{con}},\mathbf{x}_{n+1}\right)}. (4)

The distribution p^(⋅|𝐱n+1)\hat{p}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}_{n+1}) approximates the posterior distribution of the label yn+1y_{n+1} given 𝒟con\mathcal{D}_{\text{con}} and 𝐱n+1\mathbf{x}_{n+1} [24].

Conventionally, the ICL model G𝜽G_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} is pre-trained using data from TT auxiliary tasks [25]. For each task t=1,…,Tt=1,\dots,T, the context set 𝒟cont={𝐱it,yit}i=1n\mathcal{D}_{\text{con}}^{t}=\{\mathbf{x}_{i}^{t},y_{i}^{t}\}_{i=1}^{n} and the query pair (𝐱n+1t,yn+1t)(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}^{t},y_{n+1}^{t}) are drawn i.i.d. from a task-specific distribution. The ICL model parameters 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta} are optimized by minimizing a loss function ℓ(p^(⋅|𝐱n+1t),yn+1t)\ell(\hat{p}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}_{n+1}^{t}),y_{n+1}^{t}), such as the log-loss −log⁡(p^​(yn+1t|𝐱n+1t))-\log(\hat{p}(y_{n+1}^{t}|\mathbf{x}_{n+1}^{t})), averaged over all TT tasks. This yields the meta-training objective

L⁡(𝜽)=1T​∑t=1Tℓ⁡(G𝜽​(𝒟cont,𝐱n+1t),yn+1t).L(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell(G_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{con}}^{t},\mathbf{x}_{n+1}^{t}),y_{n+1}^{t}). (5)

III Optimizing ICL for Efficient Full Conformal Prediction

Classical FCP suffers from high computational complexity because it requires retraining a separate model p^y(⋅|𝐱)\hat{p}^{y}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}) for each candidate label y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y} of a given test input 𝐱n+1\mathbf{x}_{n+1}. In contrast, as discussed in Sec. II-C, an ICL model can produce a predictive distribution (4) for a new input using a set of demonstration samples without needing additional training. Based on this property, building on prior works [18, 21], in this section we introduce a novel framework for the implementation and design of ICL-based FCP using a tailored meta-learning strategy.

III-A ICL-based FCP

As illustrated in Fig. 1, the proposed E-ICL+FCP runs |𝒴||\mathcal{Y}| copies of the same Transformer model G𝜽G_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} in parallel to produce the predictive distributions p^y(⋅|𝐱)\hat{p}^{y}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}) based on each data set 𝒟y\mathcal{D}^{y} for all y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}. These models are used as explained in Sec. II-B to evaluate the NCSs {siy}i=1n+1\{s_{i}^{y}\}_{i=1}^{n+1} and sn+1ys^{y}_{n+1} and compute the FCP set predictor (3).

To compute the predictive distribution p^y(⋅|𝐱)\hat{p}^{y}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}), the n+1n+1 samples in the augmented dataset 𝒟y\mathcal{D}^{y} are each encoded as context tokens {𝐜1,…,𝐜n,𝐜n+1}\{\mathbf{c}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{c}_{n},\mathbf{c}_{n+1}\} via an embedding model h1​(⋅)h_{1}(\cdot), while the corresponding n+1n+1 queries are encoded as query tokens {𝐪1,…,𝐪n,𝐪n+1}\{\mathbf{q}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{q}_{n},\mathbf{q}_{n+1}\} via another model h2​(⋅)h_{2}(\cdot). These tokens are concatenated as [𝐜1,…,𝐜n,𝐜n+1,𝐪1,…,𝐪n,𝐪n+1][\mathbf{c}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{c}_{n},\mathbf{c}_{n+1},\mathbf{q}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{q}_{n},\mathbf{q}_{n+1}] and fed into the Transformer model G𝜽G_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}, which is composed of a number of layers.

To ensure permutation-invariance with respect to the data set 𝒟y\mathcal{D}^{y}, which is required by FCP, we implement the attention mask for all layers of the Transformer model in such a way that: (i) all context tokens can attend to each other; and (ii) each query token can attend only to the context tokens and to itself. The resulting (2​n+2)×(2​n+2)(2n+2)\times(2n+2) attention mask is given by [26]

𝐌=[contextquerycontext\Block​1−1​𝟎(n+1)×(n+1)\Block​1−1−∞⋅𝟏(n+1)×(n+1)query\Block​1−1​𝟎(n+1)×(n+1)\Block​1−1−∞​(𝟏(n+1)×(n+1)−𝐈n+1)],\small\mathbf{M}=\begin{bNiceMatrix}&\text{context}&\text{query}\\ \text{context}&\Block{1-1}{\mathbf{0}_{(n+1)\times(n+1)}}&\Block{1-1}{-\infty\cdot\mathbf{1}_{(n+1)\times(n+1)}}\\ \text{query}&\Block{1-1}{\mathbf{0}_{(n+1)\times(n+1)}}&\Block{1-1}{-\infty(\mathbf{1}_{(n+1)\times(n+1)}-\mathbf{I}_{n+1})}\end{bNiceMatrix}, (6)

where 𝟏a×b\mathbf{1}_{a\times b} represents the all-one matrix of size a×ba\times b, while 𝐈a\mathbf{I}_{a} is the a×aa\times a identity matrix.

The last n+1n+1 outputs of the Transformer model correspond to the n+1n+1 predictive distribution {p^y(⋅|𝐱i)}i=1n+1\{\hat{p}^{y}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n+1}. Based on {p^y(⋅|𝐱i)}i=1n+1\{\hat{p}^{y}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n+1}, the NCS computation and prediction set construction follow Sec. II-B as explained above.

III-B Enhanced ICL-Based FCP

Conventional ICL models are not designed for computing NCS values, and thus they often produce overly large predictive sets. Inspired by [13], which addressed SCP, we aim to design a pre-training procedure that directly minimizes the expected size of the FCP predictive set (3).

III-B1 Meta-Training Setting

As discussed in Sec. II-C, assume the availability of data from TT auxiliary tasks. The goal is to optimize the parameter vector 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta} of the Transformer model G𝜽G_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} so as to minimize the average predictive set size. Hereafter, we denote the predictive set generated by ICL-based FCP for task tt as 𝒞𝜽​(𝐱n+1t)\mathcal{C}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}^{t}_{n+1}), emphasizing the dependence on parameters 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta}. According to (3), the predictive set size can be expressed as

|𝒞𝜽​(𝐱n+1t)|=∑y∈𝒴𝟙​(sn+1t,y⩽Q1−α​({sit,y}i=1n+1)),|\mathcal{C}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}^{t}_{n+1})|=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\mathds{1}(s_{n+1}^{t,y}\leqslant Q_{1-\alpha}(\{s_{i}^{t,y}\}_{i=1}^{n+1})), (7)

where 𝟙​(⋅)\mathds{1}(\cdot) is the indicator function and the NCSs for task tt are denoted as {sit,y}\{s_{i}^{t,y}\} and sn+1t,ys_{n+1}^{t,y}. Therefore, one could in principle address the meta-learning problem

min⁡∑t=1T𝜽⁡|𝒞𝜽​(𝐱n+1t)|\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}|\mathcal{C}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}^{t})| (8)

of minimizing the average predictive set size across all tasks. However, this is challenging due to the non-differentiability of the objective (7). To address this issue, in a manner similar to [13], we introduce a smooth approximation of the objective (8) in the rest of this section.

III-B2 Soft Quantile, Soft Indicator, and Differentiable Meta-Training Function

The soft (1−α)(1-\alpha)-quantile of the set z1,…,znz_{1},\dots,z_{n} is defined as [16]

Q^1−α​({zi}i=1n)=∑j=1nzj​e−ρ1−α(zj;{zj}j=1n)/cq∑i=1ne−ρ1−α(zi;{zj}j=1n)/cq,\hat{Q}_{1-\alpha}\left(\{z_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}\right)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}z_{j}\frac{e^{-\rho_{1-\alpha}(z_{j};\{z_{j}\}_{j=1}^{n})/c_{q}}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}e^{-\rho_{1-\alpha}(z_{i};\{z_{j}\}_{j=1}^{n})/c_{q}}}, (9)

where parameter cq>0c_{q}>0 controls the smoothness of function (9), with a larger cqc_{q} yielding a larger smoothness level. The function ρ1−α​(z,{zj}j=1n)\rho_{1-\alpha}(z;\{z_{j}\}_{j=1}^{n}) in (9) denotes the pinball loss, which is given by

ρ1−α​(z,{zj}j=1n)=α​∑j=1n[z−zj]++(1−α)​∑j=1n[zj−z]+,\rho_{1-\alpha}(z;\{z_{j}\}_{j=1}^{n})=\alpha\sum_{j=1}^{n}[\,z-z_{j}\,]_{+}+(1-\alpha)\sum_{j=1}^{n}[\,z_{j}-z\,]_{+},

with [x]+=max⁡(x,0)[x]_{+}=\max(x,0).

Furthermore, given a threshold condition r⩽τr\leqslant\tau, the soft indicator function σ⁡(r,τ)\sigma(r,\tau) is defined as 1/(1+e−(r−τ)/κ){1}/{(1+e^{-(r-\tau)/\kappa})}, where κ>0\kappa>0 controls the sharpness of the transition. As κ→0\kappa\to 0, the function σ⁡(r,τ)\sigma(r,\tau) approaches the hard indicator function 𝟙​(r⩽τ)\mathds{1}(r\leqslant\tau).

Using the soft (1−α)(1-\alpha)-quantile and soft indicator, a smooth surrogate for the meta-training loss (8) is obtained as

Lineff​(𝜽)=∑t=1T∑y∈𝒴σ⁡(sn+1t,y,Q^1−α​({sit,y}i=1n+1)).L_{\text{ineff}}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\sigma(s_{n+1}^{t,y},\hat{Q}_{1-\alpha}(\{s_{i}^{t,y}\}_{i=1}^{n+1})). (10)

To promote inclusion of the true label yn+1ty_{n+1}^{t} in the predictive set, driving the corresponding value of the soft indicator towards 1, we incorporate in the meta-training criterion also the classification-related term [13]

Lclass​(𝜽)=∑t=1T(1−σ⁡(sn+1t,yn+1t,Q^1−α​({sit,y}i=1n+1))).L_{\text{class}}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\Big(1-\sigma\!\left(s_{n+1}^{t,y_{n+1}^{t}},\hat{Q}_{1-\alpha}(\{s_{i}^{t,y}\}_{i=1}^{n+1})\right)\Big). (11)

Overall, the meta-training objective for the Transformer model G𝜽G_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} is given by

L⁡(𝜽)=Lineff​(𝜽)+λ​Lclass​(𝜽),L(\boldsymbol{\theta})=L_{\text{ineff}}(\boldsymbol{\theta})+\lambda L_{\text{class}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}), (12)

where λ>0\lambda>0 is a hyperparameter balancing the two loss terms.

IV Experiments

In this section, we evaluate the proposed E-ICL+FCP against ICL+FCP [18] and a range of baselines spanning joint learning, meta-learning, and ICL, under both SCP and FCP. Results are reported on a synthetic task [27] and an image classification task [28].

IV-A Benchmarks

We compare E-ICL+FCP with baselines differing in: (i) learning paradigm, (ii) calibration strategy, and (iii) design criterion: (i) Learning paradigm: Besides ICL, we consider joint learning (JL), which trains a single model across all tasks, and meta-learning via MAML [29], which adapts task-specific models. (ii) Calibration strategy: Both SCP and FCP are considered. (iii) Design criterion: We contrast standard CP-agnostic objectives (based on log-loss) with the CP-aware objective (12). All schemes designed in (12) are referred with the prefix “E-”. This results in the following schemes: JL+SCP, E-JL+SCP, MAML+SCP, E-MAML+SCP, MAML+FCP, E-MAML+FCP, ICL+SCP, E-ICL+SCP, and ICL+FCP [18].

IV-B Symbol Demodulation

Task description: We start with a synthetic example of practical engineering relevance, namely symbol demodulation in wireless communication [27]. The transmitted symbol yy is from the QPSK constellation 𝒴={−1−j,−1+j,1+j,1−j}\mathcal{Y}=\{-1-j,-1+j,1+j,1-j\}, where jj is the complex unit and |𝒴|=K=4|\mathcal{Y}|=K=4. The received sample is x=ej​ϕ​f​(y)+vx=e^{j\phi}f(y)+v, where v∼𝒞​𝒩​(0,γ−1)v\sim\mathcal{CN}(0,\gamma^{-1}) and γ\gamma denotes the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), where the function f⁡(⋅)f(\cdot) models task-specific deterministic receiver’s impairments. Specifically, following [30] this is modeled as f⁡(y)=y¯I+j​y¯Qf(y)=\bar{y}_{\mathrm{I}}+j\bar{y}_{\mathrm{Q}}, where

[y¯Iy¯Q]=[1+ϵ001−ϵ]​[cos⁡δ−sin⁡δ−sin⁡δcos⁡δ]​[yIyQ],\begin{bmatrix}\bar{y}_{\mathrm{I}}\\ \bar{y}_{\mathrm{Q}}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1+\epsilon&0\\ 0&1-\epsilon\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\cos\delta&-\sin\delta\\ -\sin\delta&\cos\delta\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}y_{\text{I}}\\ y_{\text{Q}}\end{bmatrix}, (13)

with (yI,yQ)(y_{\text{I}},y_{\text{Q}}) being the real and imaginary parts of yy. The task-specific parameters are (ϕ,ϵ,δ,γ)(\phi,\epsilon,\delta,\gamma), where ϕ∼Uniform​(0,2​π)\phi\sim\text{Uniform}(0,2\pi), ϵ∼Uniform​(0,0.3)\epsilon\sim\text{Uniform}(0,0.3), δ∼Uniform​(0,π/6)\delta\sim\text{Uniform}(0,\pi/6), and 10​log10⁡(γ)∼Uniform​(0,10)10\log_{10}(\gamma)\sim\text{Uniform}(0,10).

Network architectures and training: For ICL-based schemes, we adopt a six-layer Transformer, with an input dimension of 16, two attention heads, and a feed-forward network dimension of 1024, with projectors h1​(⋅)h_{1}(\cdot) and h2​(⋅)h_{2}(\cdot) implemented as linear layers. For the remaining baselines, we employ a four-layer feedforward neural network.

The dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} consists of n=19n=19 examples. For SCP, these are split SCP into a training set of size l=10l=10 and a calibration set of size m=9m=9. Training and validation leverage 256 tasks each. Each task is characterized by 50 i.i.d. realizations of data (𝒟,xn+1)(\mathcal{D},x_{n+1}). Finally testing uses 512 tasks with 50 i.i.d. realizations of data 𝒟\mathcal{D}, and 10 additional i.i.d. input xn+1x_{n+1} samples. All schemes are trained using an initial learning rate of 0.0002 with a CosineAnnealingLR scheduler (50 iterations, minimum 0.00002) [31] and are trained for 200 epochs.

Results:

As shown in Fig. 2, all schemes achieve coverage rates around the prescribed level 1−α=0.91-\alpha=0.9. FCP-based schemes yield smaller predictive sets than their SCP-based counterparts, while schemes optimized with CP-aware loss also produce smaller predictive sets compared to those trained with cross-entropy loss. The proposed E-ICL+FCP method achieves the smallest predictive sets, with an average size of 1.216, which is a 6.99% reduction compared to the state-of-the-art ICL+FCP.

Table I compares the calibration-phase computational complexity by reporting the number of model training steps and prediction evaluations required by different schemes for rr test inputs. We also report the average running time per test input (r=1r=1), encompassing both training and evaluation, on a computing platform equipped with a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPU and an Intel(R) Xeon(R) Gold 6240 CPU. The proposed E-ICL+FCP is seen to offer the best performance-complexity trade-off, producing the smallest predictive sets with relatively low running time.

IV-C CIFAR-FS Image Classification

Task description: The CIFAR-FS dataset [28] consists of 100 object classes, each containing 600 RGB images of size 32×3232\times 32. Each task is a binary classification problem involving images from two randomly selected classes. 64 classes are used for meta-training, 16 for validation, and 20 for meta-testing, following the standard few-shot classification protocol.

Network architectures and training: The network architectures adopted in ICL-based schemes are unified as a six-layer Transformer encoder, with an input dimension of 128, four attention heads, and a feed-forward network dimension of 1024. The projectors h1​(⋅)h_{1}(\cdot) and h2​(⋅)h_{2}(\cdot) are implemented as a hybrid 2D CNN followed by a linear layer, and a linear layer, respectively.

We consider a number of examples n=19n=19 for the dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D}, which is split by SCP into a training set of size l=10l=10 and a calibration set of size m=9m=9. Training uses 256 tasks with 50 i.i.d. realizations of (𝒟,𝐱n+1)(\mathcal{D},\mathbf{x}_{n+1}) each; validation uses 120 tasks of same form; while testing uses 128 tasks with 50 i.i.d. realizations of 𝒟\mathcal{D}, and 10 additional i.i.d. 𝐱n+1\mathbf{x}_{n+1} samples per realization. For training, we adopt the same schedule as in the previous example.

Results: As in the previous example, the JL-based schemes produce large predictive sets, while the MAML-based schemes are severely limited by their high complexity, hence, we focus on the ICL-based schemes only. The results in Fig. 3 are consistent with the previous example, showing that FCP-based schemes achieve smaller predictive sets than SCP-based schemes. Moreover, the CP-aware training further reduces the predictive set size achieved by the ICL models. In particular, the proposed E-ICL+FCP attains an average predictive set size of 1.091, representing a 5.73% reduction relative to ICL+FCP.

V Conclusions

In this paper, we have proposed an efficient full conformal prediction framework based on in-context learning. The model employs a permutation-invariant Transformer architecture and is pre-trained with a CP-aware loss. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed scheme guarantees coverage while reducing inefficiency and computational cost compared to existing CP methods. Future work may explore extensions to regression tasks and to larger-scale real-world applications.

Supplementary Material (Appendix)

-A Proof of Permutation-Invariance

Firstly, we prove the permutation invariance for a single encoder layer with mask 𝐌\mathbf{M} in (6).

Denote by 𝐇(e−1)∈ℝp×(2​n+2)\mathbf{H}^{(e-1)}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times(2n+2)} the output of the (e−1)(e-1)-th encoder layer, which also serves as the input to the ee-th encoder layer, where pp is the dimension of the hidden state. Among its 2​n+22n{+}2 columns, the first n+1n{+}1 correspond to the context embeddings, and the last n+1n{+}1 correspond to the query embeddings. Then, the output of the ee-th encoder layer, 𝐇(e)\mathbf{H}^{(e)}, is given by

𝐇(e)\displaystyle\mathbf{H}^{(e)} =𝐇(e−1)+MHA​(LN​(𝐇(e−1)),𝐌)\displaystyle=\mathbf{H}^{(e-1)}+\text{MHA}\!\left(\text{LN}(\mathbf{H}^{(e-1)}),\mathbf{M}\right)
+FFN​(LN​(𝐇(e−1)+MHA​(LN​(𝐇(e−1)),𝐌))),\displaystyle\quad+\text{FFN}\!\left(\text{LN}\!\big(\mathbf{H}^{(e-1)}+\text{MHA}(\text{LN}(\mathbf{H}^{(e-1)}),\mathbf{M})\big)\right), (14)

where MHA​(⋅)\text{MHA}(\cdot), FFN​(⋅)\text{FFN}(\cdot), and LN​(⋅)\text{LN}(\cdot) denote the multi-head attention mechanism, the feed-forward network, and the layer normalization function, respectively.

Introduce π∈Perm⁡(n+1)\pi\in\mathrm{Perm}(n+1) be a permutation of the n+1n{+}1 sample indices, and let 𝐏π\mathbf{P}_{\pi} be the corresponding permutation matrix. Define the block permutation

𝚷≜diag⁡(𝐏π,𝐈n+1)∈{0,1}(2​n+2)×(2​n+2),\boldsymbol{\Pi}\triangleq\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{P}_{\pi},\mathbf{I}_{n+1})\in\{0,1\}^{(2n+2)\times(2n+2)}, (15)

which permutes the context embeddings. It is straightforward to verify that

𝚷⊤​𝐌​𝚷=𝐌.\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\top}\mathbf{M}\,\boldsymbol{\Pi}=\mathbf{M}. (16)

The permuted input is 𝐇~(e−1)=𝐇(e−1)​𝚷\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}^{(e-1)}=\mathbf{H}^{(e-1)}\boldsymbol{\Pi}. Fed with 𝐇~(e−1)\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}^{(e-1)}, the output of the ee-th encoder layer, 𝐇~(e)\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}^{(e)}, is given by

𝐇~(e)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}^{(e)} =𝐇~(e−1)+MHA​(LN​(𝐇~(e−1)),𝐌)\displaystyle=\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}^{(e-1)}+\text{MHA}\!\left(\text{LN}(\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}^{(e-1)}),\mathbf{M}\right)
+FFN​(LN​(𝐇~(e−1)+MHA​(LN​(𝐇~(e−1)),𝐌))).\displaystyle\quad+\text{FFN}\!\left(\text{LN}\!\big(\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}^{(e-1)}+\text{MHA}(\text{LN}(\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}^{(e-1)}),\mathbf{M})\big)\right). (17)

Note that LN​(⋅)\text{LN}(\cdot), FFN​(⋅)\text{FFN}(\cdot), and the residual connections act independently on each embedding, and therefore commute with permutations, since they apply pointwise transformations across embeddings.

Regardless of MHA⁡(⋅)\mathrm{MHA}(\cdot), we take the single-head attention as an example, since each head is computed independently and the multi-head case is obtained by concatenation of such heads followed by a linear projection. Denote 𝐅(e)=LN⁡(𝐇(e))\mathbf{F}^{(e)}=\mathrm{LN}(\mathbf{H}^{(e)}), 𝐅~(e)=LN⁡(𝐇~(e))=𝐅(e)​𝚷\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}^{(e)}=\mathrm{LN}(\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}^{(e)})=\mathbf{F}^{(e)}\boldsymbol{\Pi}. Then, the corresponding query, key, and value matrices are given by

𝐐(e)\displaystyle\mathbf{Q}^{(e)} =𝐖Q(e)​𝐅(e),\displaystyle=\mathbf{W}_{Q}^{(e)}\mathbf{F}^{(e)}, 𝐊(e)\displaystyle~\mathbf{K}^{(e)} =𝐖K(e)​𝐅(e),\displaystyle=\mathbf{W}_{K}^{(e)}\mathbf{F}^{(e)}, 𝐕(e)\displaystyle~\mathbf{V}^{(e)} =𝐖V(e)​𝐅(e),\displaystyle=\mathbf{W}_{V}^{(e)}\mathbf{F}^{(e)},
𝐐~(e)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathbf{Q}}^{(e)} =𝐖Q(e)​𝐅~(e),\displaystyle=\mathbf{W}_{Q}^{(e)}\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}^{(e)}, 𝐊~(e)\displaystyle~\widetilde{\mathbf{K}}^{(e)} =𝐖K(e)​𝐅~(e),\displaystyle=\mathbf{W}_{K}^{(e)}\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}^{(e)}, 𝐕~(e)\displaystyle~\widetilde{\mathbf{V}}^{(e)} =𝐖V(e)​𝐅~(e),\displaystyle=\mathbf{W}_{V}^{(e)}\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}^{(e)}, (18)

where 𝐖Q(e),𝐖K(e),𝐖V(e)\mathbf{W}_{Q}^{(e)},\mathbf{W}_{K}^{(e)},\mathbf{W}_{V}^{(e)} are the weight matrices of the query, key, and value projections, respectively. Also, it holds that

𝐐~(e)=𝐐(e)​𝚷,𝐊~(e)=𝐊(e)​𝚷,𝐕~(e)=𝐕(e)​𝚷.\widetilde{\mathbf{Q}}^{(e)}=\mathbf{Q}^{(e)}\boldsymbol{\Pi},~\widetilde{\mathbf{K}}^{(e)}=\mathbf{K}^{(e)}\boldsymbol{\Pi},~\widetilde{\mathbf{V}}^{(e)}=\mathbf{V}^{(e)}\boldsymbol{\Pi}. (19)

Following, the attention logits holds

𝐋~(e)=𝐐~(e)⊤​𝐊~(e)dk=𝚷⊤​𝐐(e)⊤​𝐊(e)​𝚷dk=𝚷⊤​𝐋(e)​𝚷,\widetilde{\mathbf{L}}^{(e)}=\frac{\widetilde{\mathbf{Q}}^{(e)\top}\widetilde{\mathbf{K}}^{(e)}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}=\frac{\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\top}\mathbf{Q}^{(e)\top}\mathbf{K}^{(e)}\boldsymbol{\Pi}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}=\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\top}\mathbf{L}^{(e)}\boldsymbol{\Pi}, (20)

where dkd_{k} is the dimension of the key. Together with (16), the masked logits satisfy

𝐋~(e)+𝐌=𝚷⊤​(𝐋(e)+𝐌)​𝚷.\widetilde{\mathbf{L}}^{(e)}+\mathbf{M}=\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\top}(\mathbf{L}^{(e)}+\mathbf{M})\boldsymbol{\Pi}. (21)

Then, the attention matrices 𝐀(e)\mathbf{A}^{(e)}, 𝐀~(e)\widetilde{\mathbf{A}}^{(e)} holds

𝐀~(e)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathbf{A}}^{(e)} =Softmax​(𝐋~(e)+𝐌)\displaystyle=\text{Softmax}\!\big(\widetilde{\mathbf{L}}^{(e)}+\mathbf{M}\big)
=(a)Softmax​(𝚷⊤​(𝐋(e)+𝐌)​𝚷)\displaystyle\mathop{=}^{(a)}\text{Softmax}\!\big(\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\top}(\mathbf{L}^{(e)}+\mathbf{M})\boldsymbol{\Pi}\big)
=(b)𝚷⊤​Softmax​(𝐋(e)+𝐌)​𝚷\displaystyle\mathop{=}^{(b)}\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\top}\text{Softmax}\!\big(\mathbf{L}^{(e)}+\mathbf{M}\big)\boldsymbol{\Pi}
=𝚷⊤​𝐀(e)​𝚷.\displaystyle=\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\top}\mathbf{A}^{(e)}\,\boldsymbol{\Pi}. (22)

Here, step (a) follows from the fact that the Softmax​(⋅)\text{Softmax}(\cdot) operation is applied column-wise, and step (b) holds since the Softmax operation on a single column is permutation-equivariant.

For a single attention head, let 𝐎(e)\mathbf{O}^{(e)} and 𝐎~(e)\widetilde{\mathbf{O}}^{(e)} denote the outputs with and without permuted inputs, respectively. Then it holds that

𝐎~(e)=𝐕~(e)​𝐀~(e)=(𝐕(e)​𝚷)​(𝚷⊤​𝐀(e)​𝚷)=𝐎(e)​𝚷.\widetilde{\mathbf{O}}^{(e)}=\widetilde{\mathbf{V}}^{(e)}\widetilde{\mathbf{A}}^{(e)}=\big(\mathbf{V}^{(e)}\boldsymbol{\Pi}\big)\big(\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\top}\mathbf{A}^{(e)}\boldsymbol{\Pi}\big)=\mathbf{O}^{(e)}\boldsymbol{\Pi}. (23)

Thus, each attention head is permutation-equivariant. The same relation holds for multi-head attention and its output projection:

MHA⁡(LN​(𝐇(e)​𝚷),𝐌)=MHA⁡(LN​(𝐇(e)),𝐌)​𝚷.\mathrm{MHA}(\text{LN}(\mathbf{H}^{(e)}\boldsymbol{\Pi}),\mathbf{M})=\mathrm{MHA}(\text{LN}(\mathbf{H}^{(e)}),\mathbf{M})\,\boldsymbol{\Pi}. (24)

Combined with LN​(⋅)\text{LN}(\cdot), FFN​(⋅)\text{FFN}(\cdot), and the residual connections, we have the following

𝐇~(e)=𝐇(e)​𝚷,\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}^{(e)}=\mathbf{H}^{(e)}\,\boldsymbol{\Pi}, (25)

which implies that the query outputs are invariant to any permutation over the context embeddings.

Finally, since permutation invariance is preserved under composition of permutation-invariant layers, our employed Transformer with EE cascaded encoder layers under the mask 𝐌\mathbf{M} is permutation-invariant.
